title: Velouté de potiron
subtitle: French pumpkin velouté
excerpt: Smooth, golden pumpkin soup made with roasted pumpkin or butternut squash, onion, and chicken stock, blended until velvety and finished with crème fraîche and a little nutmeg. An autumn staple across France.
sourceNotes: Velouté de potiron (pumpkin velouté) is a classic French domestic soup widely documented in French culinary literature from Escoffier onward. Potiron (pumpkin) soups appear throughout French regional cookbooks from the Burgundy and Loire regions. The method is standard in the French culinary tradition.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze before adding cream. Defrost, reheat gently, add cream to finish.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles or trebles well. A good large-batch soup for autumn.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be made the day before and gently reheated.

content.text: Velouté de potiron is the soup of the French autumn. It is simple to make, cheap, and reliably good. Roasting the pumpkin before blending it into the soup adds depth and sweetness that plain-simmered pumpkin lacks. The result is the colour of a harvest field and silky enough to serve in small glasses as an amuse-bouche before a dinner party, or in large bowls with crusty bread as a weeknight supper.

items.prepNote: or butternut squash, peeled, deseeded, cut into 4 cm chunks
hot; vegetable stock for a vegetarian version

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C (fan 180°C). Toss the pumpkin chunks, onion, and garlic cloves with the olive oil on a large baking tray. Season with salt and pepper. Roast for 30 minutes until tender and starting to caramelise at the edges.
Squeeze the roasted garlic out of its skin. Transfer the pumpkin, onion, and garlic to a large saucepan. Pour in the hot stock and bring to a simmer.
Blend the soup until completely smooth. Return to the pan, stir in the crème fraîche, and heat through gently. Season with salt, pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg. Serve hot.

items.cause: No seasoning during roasting, or no stock depth
items.fix: Season the vegetables generously before roasting. Use a well-made stock rather than water.

items.cause: Pumpkin to stock ratio is off, or blending has thickened it
items.fix: Add extra hot stock or hot water and blend again until the consistency is right.

content.text: Pumpkin soup appears across France from September through to November, wherever the large orange potiron pumpkins appear at market stalls. The French version is smoother and less spiced than its British or American counterparts: no chilli, no ginger, no coconut milk. Just pumpkin, stock, a little cream, and the faintest grate of nutmeg. It is served as a first course before a roast, or as a light supper with a thick slice of pain de campagne.
